# Copper November 2009 

- During November official 3-month quotes rose steadily from the month’s low of $6416/t on the 3<sup>rd</sup> to the month’s peak of $6950/t on the 23<sup>rd</sup> , a new 14-month high.  Whilst prices rose overall it was a month of two halves.  From the start of the month to the 13<sup>th</sup> the price was range bound fluctuating between $6580/t at the end of October and $6490/t on the 12<sup>th</sup> .  From the 12<sup>th</sup> to the 23<sup>rd</sup> of the month, 3M LME quotes rose by a net $480/t.  Prices were supported by industrial action and ongoing wage negotiations and increased interest from the fund community, the extent of which was highlighted by LME open interest which reached its highest level ever. 

- The disconnect between copper prices and market fundamentals widened significantly during the month.  This was underlined by official quotes reaching pre-crisis levels during the month despite exchange inventories rising to their highest level in almost six years, weaker physical premia in most consuming regions, and China, where demand is strongest, remaining awash with metal. 

- Demand for copper around the globe has remained mixed.  As a consequence we have lowered our Western European forecasts while we have raised our estimates for Africa and Asia.  Stronger than previously anticipated growth thus far this year in Egypt, Malaysia and South Korea was responsible for the uplift.  We now forecast that global refined copper demand will fall by 4.8% this year before recovering by 5.3% in 2010 and 5.9% in 2011. 

- There has been some progress in the Mating Season with reports of numbers being tabled between BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Escondida and its Japanese counterparts.  According to trade rumour the Chilean miner’s second round opening offer was $40/t & 4c/lb.  In response, the initial counter offers from the Japanese buyers have seemingly ranged from $60-65/t & 6.0-6.5c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Official prices trend upwards during November** During November official 3-month quotes rose steadily from the month’s low of $6416/t on the 3<sup>rd</sup> to the month’s peak of

$6950/t on the 23<sup>rd</sup> , a new 14-month high.  Whilst prices rose overall it was a month of two halves.  From the start of the month to the 13<sup>th</sup> the price was range bound fluctuating between $6580/t at the end of October and $6490/t on the 12<sup>th</sup> .  From the 12<sup>th</sup> to the 23<sup>rd</sup> of the month, 3M LME quotes rose by a net $480/t.  The relatively lacklustre performance during the first two weeks of the month was a result of the conflicting impact of concerns surrounding the fragility of the recovery following the release of disappointing macro economic data which pushed prices lower and the support for prices created by a depreciating dollar.  From the 13<sup>th</sup> onwards prices were pushed higher as buyers were encouraged by positive economic data from China and the US and growing concerns over the outcome of wage negotiations at several mines. 

**Chinese economy strengthens** China’s industrial production (IP) in October increased by 16.1% from a year earlier, the fastest rate so far this year.  This compared with an annual gain of 13.9% in September.  Market participants were particularly encouraged by the news that substantial domestic growth offset a 7.3% year on year decline in the export component of IP.  The positive spin on this data is that China’s economic growth is becoming less reliant on export demand from economies that continue to falter which will bode well for future economic (and metal demand) growth in China.  Meanwhile in the US, retail sales in October exceeded expectations.  According to the US Department of Commerce October retail sales increased by 1.4% from a month earlier, with auto related sales increasing by 7.8% month-on-month and 3% year on year although it must be pointed out that these uplifts are from very low bases in 2008. This was encouraging because it helped to dispel fears that auto production and sales would stagnate once government support was removed. 

**Supply issues continue to provide price support** Industrial action and ongoing wage negotiations again provided major price support in November.  In Zambia mine production at the Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) was disrupted for three days between the 10<sup>th</sup> and 13<sup>th</sup> as workers pushed for better wage and service conditions.  Meanwhile in Chile, industrial action at BHP Billiton’s 200kt/a Spence copper mine finally ended on Wednesday 25<sup>th</sup> .  Despite an end to the strike BHP Billiton reported that production at the mine is not expected to return to normal levels until January next year. Also in Chile, 70% of workers at Codelco’s Andina mine (225kt/a) approved a new contract offer on the 22<sup>nd</sup> ahead of the expiry date of the current contract at the end of this month and the company still has to undergo wage negotiations at its Codelco Nortй division (i.e. at Chuquicamata (535kt/a) and Radomiro Tomic (300kt/a)) before the end of the year. Elsewhere, the only other contract

negotiations outstanding of any significance are at the Antamina copper and zinc mine (335kt/a Cu) in Peru where negotiations have been underway since the end of July and at Vale Inco’s Sudbury (115kt/a Cu) and Voisey’s Bay (40kt/a Cu) nickel/copper operations which have been on strike since the summer with no sign of any settlement seemingly in the offing. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2009 Page 2 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **Increased speculative interest** Prices were also supported during the month by increased interest from the fund community, the extent of which was highlighted by LME open interest which reached its highest level ever. The establishment of new long positions and short covering were both responsible for prices moving higher. **New long positions established** The establishment of new long positions across the complex by the investment community was the result of two key factors. Firstly, commodities remain the option of choice as a hedge against a depreciating US dollar. Secondly, there is a widespread expectation that there will be a substantial inventory correction (re-stocking) in 2010 within the mature economies as demand recovers. Whilst we agree with this latter expectation we believe that the timing of this correction will be somewhat later (possibly into 2011) especially in the construction sector in markets such as the US. The effects of short covering on LME open interest was also apparent during the month with participants who had shorted the market in anticipation of falling copper prices in light of rising exchange inventories scrambling to cover their exposure as prices continued to rise. This short covering was apparent on the 23rd when prices rose by $212/t during the day, to the month’s high of $6969/t, alongside a 330 lot drop in open interest to 269.2k contracts. Since that time 3-month prices have eased slightly and are currently trading around the $6900/t level. ### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 280000 7500

**Exchange stocks rise by largest amount since January** Total Exchange stocks rose during the month by a net 84kt to 615.2kt, as of the 27th . This represented

the largest monthly increase since January this year and overall exchange stocks stand at their highest level since February 2004.  Net increases were recorded on both Comex and the LME while inventories declined on the SHFE.  The net 1.6kt fall in SHFE stocks, to 101.3kt, represented the first monthly decline since July this year.  On Comex inventories increased by a net 19.2kt to 75.4kt, their highest total since June 2004. Meanwhile inventories held in LME warehouses increased on a daily basis to 438.5kt, up 66.4kt from a month earlier. The main recipients were warehouses in both the US and South Korea where inventories rose by a net 27.4kt and 27.5kt to 255.8kt and 84.5kt respectively.  The steady gain in the US reflected ongoing weak market conditions for cathode as demand from the construction sector continued to deteriorate.  The rise may also have reflected consumers offloading unwanted material ahead of their end of year book squaring.  In South Korea the rise in inventories was partly due to material that was originally destined for China remaining in Korean warehouses.  In addition, some of the stock build resulted from metal that had been re-exported from China.  This is most likely to have come from Chinese bonded warehouses because metal re-exported from non-bonded warehouses incurs a 10% export tax, thereby making the process much less profitable (if at all).  In terms of exporting domestic (Chinese) cathodes this is discouraged given that the country is such a massive net importer of copper.  There is no VAT rebate on cathode exports (compared with 13% on semis exports) and, as mentioned, there is also a 10% export duty (unless the producer has a license to re-export metal produced from toll smelting and refining imported copper raw materials). 

**European spot activity remains slow** European spot business was, once again, very slow during the month and it was hard to determine a level of premia because of the small amount of business that took place.  However, some Chilean and grade A material from Rotterdam were reported to have traded between $60-70/t.  This was down from $70-90/t last month.  Elsewhere the price for standard grade material continued to fetch between $20-30/t as the tightness within the high-grade scrap market continued.  In contrast, premia in Italy rose during the month with Livorno warrants increasing from $60/t previously to $75/t currently.

**US premia little changed** US premia eased during the month, slipping from 3.5-4.5c/lb in October, to 3.5-4c/lb presently.  This reflected subdued business activity at both the wire rod and brass mills and also a lull ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday period.  Business was also very slow during the annual American Copper Council’s fall meeting which took place mid-month.  Normally term contracts for the following year are concluded during this meeting but this did not

occur as many consumers were unsure of their requirements for next year. **Asian premia subdued** Rising inventories in Asian warehouses this month resulted in weaker premia in the region. Metal in Singapore traded between $20-40/t, compared with $50/t last month, while in South Korea warrants fetched $15-20/t, down on last month. Meanwhile in China, cathode re-exported from bonded warehouses traded between flat to $20/t. In the long-term market Codelco increased its 2010 annual premia to its Chinese customers by $10/t to $85/t. Many appeared disgruntled with the increase and it was suggested that some consumers would not commit to term tonnage during Q1 next year preferring to meet their needs from the spot market. **Chinese October trade data as expected** Chinese refined imports in October totalled 169kt. This was the lowest monthly import figure thus far this year and was down by 40% from September’s level (283kt). However, the decline was expected in light of reduced price arbitrage opportunities from August onwards with average monthly LME prices trading above average SHFE quotes (exclusive of VAT). We would not expect refined copper imports to rise above this level over the balance of the year. Despite the decline in October, refined imports increased by 31% (+41kt) year on year in October and were up by 149% (+1.6Mt) during the first ten months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008 to 2.75Mt. For the year as a whole we estimate that refined imports will total a little over 3Mt. ### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports (kt)** 600 400

**Strong disconnect between copper prices and fundamentals** The disconnect between copper prices and market fundamentals widened significantly during the month. This was underlined by official quotes reaching pre-crisis levels during the month despite exchange inventories rising to their highest level in almost six years, weaker physical premia in most consuming regions, and China, where demand is strongest, remaining awash with metal. As a consequence of the higher price environment this month we have raised our average 2009 price forecast, lifting it from $4964/t ($2.25/lb) previously to $5076/t ($2.30/lb). We have also increased our 2009 market surplus, by ~50kt, and now forecast that supply will exceed demand by ~1Mt, which further highlights the disconnect between price behaviour and fundamentals. **Global surplus reduced in 2010 and 2011** In 2010 we forecast a much reduced global metal surplus of ~275kt, reflecting restricted supply growth (+0.9%) and fairly robust (+5.3%) demand growth (though from a low base) and an average price of $6063/t ($2.75/lb). Historically, strong first use copper

demand growth has occurred some 18 months to two years after the low-point in a recession-driven downturn in consumption. This is because many applications for copper in, for example, the construction sector, tend to be required towards the end of construction projects (plumbing, wiring, decorative items). For the world ex-China we expect this to be the case again and as such forecast that it will not be until 2011 when there will be a full recovery in demand outside of China. As a consequence, we forecast stronger growth in first use consumption in 2011, with an uplift in demand of 5.9% which will coincide with a meaningful (+4.5%) rise in refined production, resulting in a virtually balanced market, leading to a moderate increase in average prices to $6175/t ($2.80/lb). Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2009 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Japanese recovery surprises on the upside** The Japanese economy grew for the second quarter running in Q3. Data released during November showed third quarter real GDP growing by 1.2% from the previous quarter (4.8% annualised rate). The recovery was driven by strong external demand, as well as improving labour market conditions and private domestic consumption. While the data is encouraging, there are signs that much of the improvement has been due to government stimulus packages, and the possibility remains of Japan dipping back into recession in 2010. ### **Japanese monthly trade statistics** 2 8

**Exports drive Japanese recovery** External demand was once again the key driver for Japan’s economic growth, despite the strength of the yen reducing the appeal of Japanese goods to overseas buyers. Although both imports and exports remain well down from their pre-crisis levels, the recovery in exports has outstripped that of imports, resulting in a trade surplus in October of ¥807bn, the largest since early 2008. Japanese exports have benefitted greatly from overseas fiscal stimulus packages, particularly in the autos sector, and much of the export recovery has been due to Asian countries. Since the trough in January, the volume of trade to Asian economies has increased by 83% to near precrisis levels. In September, core machinery orders rose by a robust 10.5% from August, with overseas orders increasing by 26% month on month. The report showed that Japanese producers expect core orders to continue rising through the fourth quarter, despite the still uncertain outlook and that capacity utilisation in industry remains low. ### **Japanese monthly core machinery orders** 1300 Core machinery orders 20%

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2009 Page 7 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **Concerns over domestic consumption remain** Dark clouds still linger on the horizon for the Japanese economy. Improved consumer spending in Japan has largely been due to the eco-points subsidies, and consumer sentiment is yet poor. The third quarter Tankan survey showed that the majority of firms felt that their staffing levels were excessive, meaning that once the inventory adjustment wanes, further job cuts could be in the offing. Having highlighted the risks of a double-dip recession, the Japanese government announced in late November it is planning a second stimulus package for next year. **Europe shows modest signs of improvement** The euro zone economy continues to claw its way out of recession slowly. Industrial output expanded for the fifth consecutive month in September, rising by 0.3% from August, boosted by higher output of capital and non-durable consumer goods. With industrial orders in September advancing a further 1.5% from August, indications are that output will continue to expand in the coming months. However, output remains well down from pre-crisis levels. IP in September was 12.9% down from a year earlier; this is a much slower rate of contraction than the 21% in April, but still extremely weak. Also, much of the recovery to date has been spurred by fiscal stimulus packages that will expire in 2010, and inventory rebuilding, which contributed 1.5% to Germany’s 0.7% QoQ GDP growth in Q3, is a temporary boost. While a double-dip recession seems unlikely, a slowdown in growth early next year is distinctly possible. **Brazilian recovery strengthens** The recovery in Brazil’s economy gained has gained momentum, propelled by robust domestic demand. Following the sharp contraction in industrial output late last year, IP has increased in every month of 2009 through to September, and is up by 14.6% year to date. However, IP in September was still down by 8.1% from a year earlier, before the collapse in output took place. Annual IP growth is expected to have become positive by the end of 2009, and grow strongly through 2010. ### **Brazilian industrial production** 135 15%

**Strong domestic demand the driver** Policy measures have benefited the domestic industry and service sectors, allowing the economy to grow in the face of anaemic export demand. Unemployment has been in decline

since March, falling to 7.5% in October, thanks in part to the government’s temporary jobs initiative.  The Brazilian central bank cuts its benchmark interest rate from 13.75% at the end of 2008 to 8.75% in July, easing credit conditions and helping the economic recovery to gain momentum.  Perhaps most importantly, inflation in Brazil continues to fall, with the annual rate of inflation in October of 4.17% below the central inflation target.  This gives the central bank plenty of scope to keep interest rates expansionary through into 2010, aiding the economy’s transition back towards potential economic growth.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

**Global forecasts revised upwards** We have made a series of amendments to our demand estimates since our last monthly report, reflecting revisions to reported historical consumption figures as well as reported year-to-date demand numbers.  On the downside we have lowered our Western European forecasts while we have raised our estimates for Africa and Asia.  Stronger than previously anticipated growth thus far this year in Egypt, Malaysia and South Korea was responsible for the uplift.  The net effect of these changes was to increase our 2009 global refined copper consumption estimate by ~40kt to ~17.2Mt.  However, the knock-on effect of these revisions resulted in much stronger increases being made to our demand forecasts for 2010 and 2011 where they were increased by ~190kt in 2010 and 130kt in 2011 to 18Mt and 19.1Mt respectively.  The sharp rise in 2010 also reflected an upward revision to our Chinese demand estimate.  We now forecast that global refined copper demand will fall by 4.8% this year before recovering by 5.3% in 2010 and 5.9% in 2011. 

**French cathode demand remains dire** Cathode demand in France is extremely weak at the moment.  This reflects the closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant since September 17th because of strike action.  Workers are objecting to the company’s decision to close the plant at the beginning of next year.  Our sources indicated that it is now very unlikely that the plant will re-open at all.  The company recently announced that its Lens wire rod plant will take up some of the lost production by increasing its capacity to a 5-day shift, according to our sources.  By doing this the company is hoping to lift production from 165kt to 190-195kt.  However, market sources believe that this ramp up in production is questionable because the plant has never operated at this rate before.  Instead, production is more likely to reach between 175-180kt, according to our sources.  Taking the wire rod plant closure into account we now forecast that French refined copper consumption will decline by ~30% this year to 253kt, and by a further 24.5% in 2010 to 200kt. 

**Spanish copper demand down sharply** In Spain refined copper demand has fallen significantly during the year and is one of the worst

affected European economies. Deteriorating market conditions reflect the sharp contraction in construction activity. As a consequence the relatively new La Farga wire rod plant (180kt/a) which came on stream last year is currently running at only 50%, according to our sources. This is below the plant’s original plans of ramping production up to over 75% of capacity during the first three years of operation. It was also reported that production from Spain’s other two wire rod plants, Cunext (180kt/a) and SIA (57kt/a), was struggling. Reflecting this we forecast that Spain’s refined copper consumption will fall by 3.8% this year to 260kt. This reflected heavy de-stocking by the company’s customers during this time. However, our sources also informed us that since that time Aurubis’s order levels have recovered. As a consequence the company is now running at a production capacity rate of between 65-70%. Despite this improvement we still forecast a 26% decline in German refined copper consumption this year to ~1Mt as demand continues to be impacted by the downturn in the region’s construction and auto sectors. **Further deterioration in Italian demand for copper and copper alloy products** Demand for copper wire rod is also weak in Italy, reflecting deteriorating orders from the domestic construction sector. It was also reported that financial issues are causing addi

tional problems for one particular wire rod producer.  The continued slowdown in the construction sector is also continuing to hamper demand for copper and copper alloy products.  This was highlighted recently when Assomet, Italy’s Non-ferrous National Association, reported a significant decline in the production of copper bars and sections and copper tube during Q3 from a year earlier.  According to the Association, output of copper bars and sections declined by 95.5% year on year while the production of copper tube fell by 26.4%.  Copper products, overall, declined by 9.6%, to 122.8kt, while the output of copper and copper alloy products weakened by 26.4%, to 82.4kt, year on year through to September.  For the first nine months of the year the Association reported a 26.2% annual decline in the production of copper and copper alloy products to 685kt.  With this in mind we forecast a 22% decline in Italian refined copper consumption this year to ~500kt. 

**European copper fabricating plants now running at a sustainable level** According to anecdotal reports European consumers are unsure of future orders in 2010 with many of them claiming to have no clear visibility regarding future demand.  As a consequence they are ordering only 2-3 weeks ahead.  However, on a positive note many plants are running at 75% of capacity which is similar to the level reached 18 months ago and, therefore, sustainable.  Thus, while consumers are unsure of future order levels they are currently operating at a production level which they know to be sustainable and are therefore prepared to commit themselves to 50% of production capacity on term contracts, according to our sources.  This is much more positive than this time last year where many consumers were unwilling to commit on a term basis because they were unsure of how far demand was going to fall.  Next year we forecast that European refined copper consumption will recover moderately, increasing by 2.2% to just under 2.8Mt. 

**US economy still fragile** According to the US Purchasing Managers Index, manufacturing activity increased for the third consecutive month in October where the index rose from 52.6 in September to 55.7 in October.  Also encouraging was the news that the production component of the index reached its highest level since July 2004.  Despite this improvement the general consensus is that the US economy still remains very weak.  This was highlighted by the US Federal Reserve recently reporting that capacity utilisation rates across the board are down significantly.  According to PricewaterhouseCoopers, 59% of North American auto manufacturing capacity will be utilised this year, compared with 86% in 2007.  Although this is forecast to return to 2007 levels by 2012, it still leaves substantial excess capacity in the next couple of years.  Elsewhere in the auto sector US car and light vehicle output showed some improvement over September levels but was still down 13% year on year in October, to 6

**Chinese October concentrate imports slow month on month but remain up by 10% year on year** Although China’s month-on-month copper concentrate imports were considerably less (-19%) in October at 453.1kdmt these were still 10% higher than the same period last year.  On a cumulative basis the country has thus far imported 5.14Mdmt which is a rise of 19% year on year.  Taking account of this latest data, overall Chinese concentrate imports should be approximately 6.1 to 6.2Mdmt this year (~1.6Mdmt Cu).  Chile, Peru and Australia collectively account for 50% of China’s requirements and the addition of Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Mexico, the US and Canada brings the total to in excess of 75%.  According to the National Bureau of Statistics the Chinese copper smelting and refining sector experienced a 63% decline in post tax profits during the first eight months of 2009.  That said the industry overall remained profitable during this period, recording a $440Bn post tax gain, equivalent to 7.6c/lb of refined copper produced.  In addition, according to the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA) ongoing fixed asset investment within the copper smelting and refining sector increased by 5.6% year on year in the first nine months of 2009 while investment in new starts soared by almost 41% year on year during the same period.  Developments of late have seen the Guangdong Qiaoxing Group place its 100kt/a Chifeng Fubang custom smelter into trial production during November.  Construction of the $80M project, which is located in Chifeng City in Inner Mongolia, commenced in March 2008.  In addition, Liangshan Mining Co. expects to complete its new 100kt/a smelter in Sichuan province by year end with a view to commissioning in March 2010.  The project, based on IsaSmelt technology, will have taken two years to complete and will rely upon the international market for almost 90% of its feed.  Elsewhere, Baiyin Nonferrous Metals Group is spending $32M on a stage II expansion of its copper smelter/refinery complex to raise output to 200kt/a by October 2010.  Stage I, involving modernising and upgrading the existing plant and equipment, has raised output from 80kt/a to 100kt/a and was completed in October 2009 at a cost of $28M. 

**Chinese primary smelting capacity growing by 13% p.a.** The growth in China’s primary copper smelting capacity has been quite remarkable over the past seven years with an average uplift of 13% p.a.  This compares with a very modest 2.4% p.a. elsewhere in the world and an average overal

l global increase of 4% p.a. over the same time frame. The largest gains have been seen at Jiangxi Copper and Jinchuan who have both recorded a near-300kt/a increase over the period, although the rise in Jiangxi Copper’s refinery capacity has been more substantial (450kt/a) after taking account of secondary smelting capacity growth. Significant greenfield projects developed over this period include Shandong Xiangguang (200kt/a in 2007), Dongying (100kt/a in 2008), Feishang (100kt/a in 2007) and now Chifeng Fubang. Net of domestic mine production, the Chinese custom smelting industry will require almost 8Mt of concentrate imports (25% Cu) during 2010 if it is to operate at optional primary utilisation rates (88%). This year, the shortfall in imported concentrates has been ~1.5Mdmt relative to this optimal utilisation rate. In the medium term there are various smelter projects and expansions that are set to be brought on stream including Zijin Mining (200kt/a in mid 2011), Huludao (150kt/a in late 2010), Yunnan Tin (100kt/a in 2011), Xiangguang expansion (100kt/a in 2011) and Daye (230kt/a in 2012). ### **Changes in Chinese Primary Smelting Capacity: 2002 – 2010F** 3500

**BHP Billiton sees repairs at Olympic Dam completed in March 2010** BHP Billiton has confirmed that it expects repairs to Olympic Dam to be completed by the end of March 2010.  Ore is currently being extracted through the Whenan shaft at about 25% of the mine’s normal rate and the company will undertake trials involving trucking ore to surface via the decline. **Baluba mine to restart in mid December** According to China Nonferrous Metal Mining Co. operations at the Baluba mine and mill in Zambia are set to resume in mid December at an initial rate of 2kt/d of ore grading 1.4% Cu.  The operation was shut down at the end of 2008 by the former owners on account of depressed copper prices with the assets being transferred to the State.  China Nonferrous Metal Mining Co. was the successful bidder at auction for these assets. Reactivation had been delayed by the need for a mill refurbishment due to the poor state of the plant. **Six month delay seen at Tia Maria** Southern Copper expects the start up of its Tia Maria project in Peru to be delayed by around six months and is now aiming to commission it at the end of 2011.
